messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi had always prided himself on being a calm and collected individual. As a psychologist, he was trained to manage his emotions and help others navigate their own. But that all changed one night when he was brutally raped by a stranger in an abandoned building. The event shook Kofi to his core, leaving him with a sense of vulnerability he had never experienced before. In the aftermath, Kofi began to feel like he was walking around with a neon sign on his forehead, broadcasting what had happened to him for all to see. He became convinced that others could tell just by looking at him, and this feeling of exposure only intensified his growing sense of hopelessness. He started to believe that he had no future, that he would never be able to escape the trauma of that night. As a result, Kofi began to feel helpless, like he was powerless to stop bad things from happening to him. As these negative appraisals took hold, Kofi's perception of his environment changed. He started to feel like he was constantly on edge, waiting for the next attack. Being in locked or confined spaces became unbearable, as it reminded him of being trapped and helpless during the assault. Comments about sexual violence made him cringe, transporting him back to that fateful night. Even being alone with men triggered a wave of anxiety, making Kofi feel like he was walking on eggshells. Kofi's growing sense of threat only served to reinforce his negative appraisals. He became convinced that the world was a treacherous place, full of predators waiting to pounce. As a result, he started to develop strategies to cope with this perceived danger. He would position himself in rooms so that his back was against the wall, giving him a clear view of any potential threats. At night, Kofi found it difficult to fall asleep, as he needed to stay alert and vigilant for any signs of danger. Even when he knew he was safe, he couldn't shake the feeling of unease, unable to relax or let his guard down. As time went on, these habits began to take a toll on Kofi's daily life. His relationships with colleagues and friends suffered as he became increasingly withdrawn and isolated. He started to avoid situations that might trigger his anxiety, turning down social invitations and avoiding certain places. Even his work as a psychologist began to suffer, as he struggled to connect with clients who were dealing with their own trauma. It was this growing sense of disconnection that finally brought Kofi to seek help. He realized that he couldn't continue living in a state of constant hypervigilance, always waiting for the next shoe to drop. As he sat in his therapist's office, Kofi confided in her about his fears and struggles, hoping to find a way to break free from the cycle of threat and negative appraisals that had been holding him back for so long.
